language.sample_text: ระวัง — งานก่อสร้างถนน
language.script_notes: Thai script has a distinctive abundance of circles and loops, unlike Khmer (right-pointing hooks) or Lao. The baht symbol (฿) appears on pricing. Regional languages/dialects (Northern Thai, Southern Thai, Malay in the deep south) exist but Thai script dominates signage nationwide.

road_furniture.bollard_shape: Square/angular obelisk-shaped posts — similar angular bollards also appear in Laos.
road_furniture.guardrail_type: Standard steel guardrail on major highways.
road_furniture.line_paint: White outside/yellow inside center lines, sometimes striped or solid; white middle lines also common.
road_furniture.curb_style: Painted kerbs in cities; open roadside space elsewhere.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Concrete utility poles with small vertical rows of holes running up the pole are a strong Thailand tell; street-light poles often carry black-and-red or black-and-white paint at the base. PTT, Caltex, Esso, Bangchak and PTG are common fuel-station brands.

architecture.roof_style: Multi-tiered, steeply pitched, ornate roofs with upswept ends (chofa) on Buddhist temple (wat) buildings; simple corrugated metal or tile roofs on typical houses.
architecture.roof_material: Corrugated metal widespread on houses; glazed orange/green tile on temple roofs.
architecture.wall_construction: Concrete-block and stucco shophouses in towns and cities; traditional wooden stilt houses in rural areas; gilded, ornate Buddhist temple architecture with gold leaf and mosaic detailing is Thailand's most visually distinctive built form.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Brightly coloured shopfronts and signage; gold, white and vivid orange/red on temples.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Buddhist wats with gilded chedis (stupas) and ornate multi-tiered roofs; small roadside spirit houses (san phra phum) in front of homes and businesses — a strong, near-universal Thailand tell; 7-Eleven convenience stores on nearly every block.

nature.vegetation: Varies sharply by region — see regional profiles for northern hill forest, central rice paddies and southern rubber/palm plantations.
nature.terrain: Mountainous in the north (Doi Inthanon at 2,565m), a flat, fertile central plain around Bangkok, a rugged northeastern plateau (Isan), and a narrow peninsula in the south.
nature.climate_signature: Hot, humid tropical monsoon climate nationwide; lush green vegetation year-round, with regional variation in terrain and crops.

vehicles.plate_color: White plates with black text for private cars, yellow plates for taxis and commercial vehicles.
vehicles.plate_format: A digit, two Thai letters, then up to four digits (e.g. '1กก 1234'), with the province name in Thai script beneath.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Toyota Hilux and Isuzu D-Max pickup trucks are ubiquitous; tuk-tuks (three-wheeled taxis) and songthaews (converted pickup-truck shared taxis) are strong Thailand tells; motorbikes are extremely common.

google_coverage.camera_generation: Mostly Gen 3/4 official coverage, very dense.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: Dense, near-complete coverage nationwide including most rural roads — one of the best-covered countries in Southeast Asia.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared Buddhist temple architecture, similar tropical Southeast Asian vegetation and motorbike-heavy traffic
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Thailand drives on the LEFT while Cambodia drives on the right; Thai script's abundance of circles differs from Khmer's right-pointing hooks.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared Buddhist temple architecture, similar angular bollards and road furniture, related script family
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Thailand drives on the LEFT while Laos drives on the right; Thailand's road network and infrastructure are much denser and more developed.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared left-hand traffic, similar tropical peninsula vegetation and rubber/palm plantations near the southern border
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Thai script and Buddhist temples vs. Malaysia's Latin-script Malay/English signage and predominance of mosques in the north; Malaysia's plates and road furniture also differ.
